entries.title: Action card
entries.summary: Reusable run-action card with an Info panel, confirm dialog, and status.
entries.description: ActionCard is the reusable building block for rack commands. Each card carries a category badge, artwork for that category, the action's name and a one-line summary, and two buttons: Info, which opens the full description, and the action itself, which confirms before running. Clicking anywhere on the card opens Info — never the action — so a mis-click on a destructive control such as Drain or BMC Recovery costs nothing. Where nodes are selected, the confirmation lists every hostname before anything runs. A status tag reports Running, Done or Error, and the card is highlighted while its run is in flight. The cards share their appearance with the catalog-driven widgets on the Validation board.
features: Info button and card click open the full description; only the action button runs it.
Confirmation lists every selected node by name before running.
Category badge and artwork, matching the tool catalog's categories.

Test completion counts a test as done once it has a verdict, pass or fail, so it answers 'has this node been tested' rather than 'did it pass'. Two layouts: Compact tiles racks eight across as tray blocks with a per-rack good/warn/bad tally (the whole floor on one screen), Linear gives each rack a row and each node a load gauge. Both reports share one fleet sweep of per-node hardware and firmware identity — asking twice while a sweep runs joins the running job rather than starting a second one — and report progress per node. PDF is only offered when the image can render it.

Hardware and NVLink/network reports are available as persistent sections. Selecting a node shows Job IDs, categories, findings, current Slurm reason, and controls for immediate deep audits or an explicit operator mark/drain.

Persistent Node hardware status and Node network status report sections.

entries.title: Deployment Tracker
entries.summary: Bring-up progress per node, rolled up by rack, row and scalable unit, ready to publish as a static page.
entries.description: The Deployment Tracker folds everything Rack Status knows about the bring-up into one state per compute node — completed, in progress, in remediation, not started, or handed over — and lays it out on the floor: scalable unit, then row, then rack. A node is completed when its Stage 1 (single-node NCCL) and Stage 2 (single-node LLM training) have both passed; it is in remediation when a stage failed or Slurm holds it down or drained, so a node drained after passing is back on the list. entries.title: Users
entries.summary: Who can sign in; create accounts, reset passwords, disable and delete.
entries.description: Users manages the local identity store. Accounts authenticate with SRP, so the server holds a verifier and never a password — which shapes everything on this page. A new user receives a one-time password shown exactly once and must choose their own at first sign-in; a reset issues a fresh one and signs the previous holder out everywhere. A login is the principal in every audit record: it cannot be renamed, and once deleted it is retired permanently and can never be created again, because reusing it would reattribute a departed operator's history to somebody else. Disable is the reversible operation; delete is not.
features: Create a user and receive a one-time password shown once.
Reset a password, which seizes the account and ends its sessions immediately.
Disable or re-enable an account; disabling revokes sessions rather than waiting for expiry.
Delete a user, retiring the login permanently.

Prefer Disable: it ends their sessions immediately and keeps their group memberships, and it is reversible.

entries.description: Groups collect users for authorization. Groups are flat — a group holds users and never another group — so there is no nesting to reason about and no inherited membership. Membership recorded now takes effect when the policy engine lands: today authorization is permissive for every signed-in user, so a group grants nothing yet and this page is not restricting access. A group name is its identifier and cannot be changed; deleting a group removes its memberships but leaves the users untouched.

Editing membership is the highest-privilege operation on this surface, because it is how grants will be conferred.

entries.title: Policies
entries.summary: Write authorization policies and attach them to users and groups.
entries.description: Policies decide what a signed-in operator may do. Evaluation starts at an implicit deny: a request is refused unless some attached policy allows it, and any matching deny wins outright — a deny cannot be outvoted by any number of allows, at any specificity, in any file order. Policies never name principals; they are attached to users and groups as a separate relation, so granting someone access never means editing a document other people depend on. A policy that is not attached to anyone grants nothing. With no policies at all, every authenticated request is permitted and the audit trail records the engine as permissive, so writing the first policy is what starts enforcement.
features: Author policies in a JSON editor that validates against the server's own schema as you type.
Completion over the real action vocabulary, so an action name cannot be mistyped silently.
Attach a policy to a user or a group; attaching to a group reaches every member.
See which subjects hold each policy before changing or deleting it.

steps: Click 'New policy'. The template shows an allow plus a deny, which is the usual shape.

Save. The server validates again and refuses a bare '*' in an allow statement.
Click 'Attach' and pick a group. Until then the policy grants nothing.

howTo.task: Protect a rack from an existing grant
steps: Add a deny statement naming that rack, in the same policy or a separate one.
Attach it to the same subjects. A deny beats every allow, so ordering does not matter.

howTo.task: Check what a policy actually grants, before trusting it
steps: Open GET /api/policies/preview (add ?format=table for a readable grid).
It walks the whole action vocabulary, marks everything denied, then applies the policies attached to that principal exactly as the engine does — denies last and not flippable.
Each allowed entry names the resource patterns that qualify it and the policy and statement that decided, so the answer is 'yes, for these racks' rather than a bare true.

howTo.task: Let a team adopt shared boards without overwriting your tools
steps: Allow catalog.board:import together with catalog.tool:create and workflow:save.
Deny catalog.tool:update in the same policy.
Importing a shared board then creates actions the instance lacks and refuses any item that would replace one of yours; the refused item is reported as skipped and the rest still apply.

faqs.q: Why am I getting 403 when I am signed in?
faqs.a: 403 means authorization, not authentication: you are who you say you are and may not do this. Most often no attached policy grants the action. Check the audit event — it carries the deciding reason — or open GET /api/policies/preview for the whole picture for that principal. A 401 instead means the credential itself was refused, which is a different problem.

faqs.q: A deny is refusing me and I cannot see which rule.
faqs.a: Give every statement a 'sid'. The audit reason is then 'denied by <policy>/<sid>', which names the exact rule. Without a sid the verdict can only name the document.

faqs.q: A brand-new feature returns 403 for an administrator.
faqs.a: The administrators policy can be narrower than the product after an upgrade that adds actions. Run 'python backend/cli.py reconcile-admin-policy' to add the newer resource types to it.

faqs.q: My grant on one rack does not let the table load.
faqs.a: A list verb resolves to the collection sentinel '<type>:_all', and a grant on a single instance does not cover it — deliberately, because listing reveals what exists. Grant '<type>:*', which does match _all, or name _all explicitly.

tips: Attach to a group rather than to each person: one write per role, and adding someone to the team grants it by membership.
Write rack ids in lower case. Handlers that fold case have their resources folded to match, so a deny on 'rack.power:p17-r01' is what matches a request for 'P17-R01'.
Unknown fields in a policy are rejected, not ignored — a misspelled key is a typo you want to hear about rather than a rule that silently does nothing.

Full reference, with the schema field by field and worked examples: the Documentation site this deployment serves at /docs/ (Identity and authorization). The live schema and action list are also served at /api/policies/schema and /api/policies/vocabulary.

aria.label: Policies page
aria.description: Write authorization policies and attach them to users and groups.

entries.aiContext: Policies are the authorization layer. Evaluation is default-deny, deny-overrides-allow, and allow-only-on-explicit-match. Policies do not name principals: they are attached to users and groups, so cost grows with what is attached to the requesting principal rather than with the size of the whole policy set, and 'attach a policy to a user' never means editing a shared document. An unattached policy grants nothing, and with no policy file at all the engine is permissive and says so in the audit record. Actions are 'service[.subservice]:verb' (rack.power:on) and resources are '<type>:<id>' (rack.power:a01), with '<type>:_all' meaning the collection — so a grant of one rack does not confer the ability to list them. A bare '*' is refused in an allow statement because it would grant every action the product will ever have; it is permitted in a deny. Both the JSON schema and the action vocabulary are served by the API so the editor cannot accept a document the server would reject.

faqs.q: Do I put the script in the platform folder if the tool supports GB200 and GB300?
faqs.a: Only if the script itself differs per platform. The compatibility list decides which clusters are offered the tool; it does not choose the folder. A script that runs on both belongs in the shared defaults (via a merge request) or in custom/ if you wrote it for this deployment.

faqs.q: Why can I not edit multi-platform/ or the platform folders?
faqs.a: They ship with the app and every project on this server shares them, so an edit changes another customer's run — and the next deploy overwrites it. Put your own script in custom/, change a project's copy in project-<id>/, or open a merge request to change what ships.

faqs.q: My tool fails with 'no such file'. Where should the script be?
faqs.a: On the head node, under one of the four layers, with exactly the basename you registered. Copying it to the machine running the dashboard is the usual mistake.

tips: A compiled binary (a nccl-tests build, say) does not live in the script tree: wrap it in a script, or point an env-key override at its absolute path.

faqs.q: Why did Documentation used to show the login screen, or 'not authorized'?
faqs.a: It was a gated route reached by a plain link, which is two problems. A plain navigation does not go through the app's fetch layer, so it never got the session renewal that keeps the rest of the app signed in, and the link failed about an hour after signing in. Separately, an administrators policy written before the docs service existed refused administrators outright. /docs/ is public now: the documentation is the same text anybody can read in the repository, so gating it protected nothing and broke reading it in two different ways.

faqs.q: Is it a problem that the documentation needs no sign-in?
faqs.a: It is the point: an external reader or an air-gapped operator can read it, and it cannot log anybody out. The route serves only static files from the Sphinx build, sets no cookie, reads no credential and touches no cluster state, and everything else still requires authentication. backend/tests/test_docs_are_public.py holds each of those.

faqs.q: Why is it not a new browser tab any more?
faqs.a: The desktop shell has no browser tab to open, so a new tab walked you out of the application entirely. 'Open in a new window' is still there when you want it.

faqs.q: The page says the documentation has not been built. What now?
faqs.a: static/docs is a build artifact, so a developer tree or a backend-only deployment can genuinely lack it. Build it with sphinx-build -W --keep-going -b html docs static/docs; the container image builds it already.

It edits the Manager/app-server addresses, the app-server SSH connection the reconcile runs over (the app server is its own host, not the cluster control node), the compute-peer inventory pattern and source path, install/storage paths, and the rollout defaults (rollout_wave_size, rollout_parallelism, rollout_poll_seconds, rollout_max_launches, rollout_max_unreachable, rollout_timeout_seconds, rollout_strategy sequential|rack-staged, rollout_stages ladder ending at 100%, rollout_fill_wave_size where 0 = the wave size, rollout_stall_seconds default 600 where 0 turns stall handling off, rollout_download_timeout_seconds default 3600 -- the hard limit each node enforces on one download). Secrets are generated on the app server, never stored. It names provisioning blockers and exposes a gated Provision action that starts a reconcile workflow run.

entries.title: Catalog
entries.summary: Edit the active cluster's catalog — the container images (tasks) P2P can distribute — and pin each one to the exact file staged on the origin.
entries.description: The Catalog is the list of distributable images for the active cluster, stored by Rack Status as the source of truth. Each entry is a bare *.sqsh filename, a display name, its size in bytes and a SHA-256 pin. Every node verifies a download against that pin, so the pin must match the file staged on the origin byte for byte; a blank pin marks an image added but not yet imported. Saving does not touch the fleet: a Sync operation (Artifact Fleet) projects the catalog onto the cluster's manifest and the nodes, and each node also refreshes its copy of the catalog every 15 minutes. If no catalog has been authored yet, the editor opens with the cluster's current manifest.
features: Per-image order, name, *.sqsh filename, size and SHA-256 pin
Validation of filenames (bare names only, never a path) and pins (64 hex characters, or blank)
Opens with the cluster's current manifest when nothing has been authored yet

A roster name is free text (it may contain spaces); node entries must be bare hostnames. An operation that names a roster that no longer exists is refused before it reaches the fleet.

entries.title: Campaigns
entries.summary: Saved distributions — an image, a roster and optional pacing — that you name once and launch to the fleet on demand.
entries.description: A campaign pairs one catalog image with a roster (or the whole fleet) and optional pacing overrides: wave size, parallelism, poll interval, launch and unreachable limits, and timeout. A pacing field left at 0 inherits the cluster's rollout default from Dragonfly Settings. A campaign can also choose its wave plan: Sequential slices the roster in order, Rack-staged gives every rack one copy first and then grows every rack up a stage ladder (by default to half, then full) so new nodes pull from rack-mates rather than the app server's seeds; Cluster default uses the plan set in Dragonfly Settings. Launching a campaign asks for confirmation, then queues a distribute operation tagged with the campaign's name; it preheats the seeds and rolls the image out wave by wave, and its progress and log appear in Artifact Fleet. Only one operation runs at a time, so a launch is refused while another is in flight. Re-launching is safe: nodes that already hold the pinned image are skipped.
features: Image × roster × pacing, saved per cluster
Confirm-before-launch, with a link to the launched operation's log
Pacing overrides where 0 inherits the cluster default
Runs tagged with the campaign name in the operations history

steps: Add and pin the image in Catalog, then run Sync.

tips: A launch is refused while another operation is running; wait for it to finish.
Nodes deferred as unreachable in one run are picked up by launching the same campaign again.
For big images, Rack-staged with a ladder like 1, 50%, 100% keeps most pulls inside racks; a finer ladder (1, 2, 4, 8, 100%) spreads the load further.
A download that stops writing is restarted after the stall window (Stall, default 10 minutes) rather than holding the whole wave until its timeout.

aria.label: Campaigns
aria.description: Saved image distributions that can be launched to a roster or the whole fleet.

entries.aiContext: Campaigns are saved distributions for the active cluster's NVIS-P2P instance (backend P2pCampaigns, GET/PUT /api/p2p/campaigns). A campaign names a catalog image, a roster (blank = whole fleet) and optional pacing overrides (wave_size, parallelism, poll_seconds, max_launches, max_unreachable, timeout_seconds, fill_wave_size, stall_seconds, download_timeout_seconds; 0 inherits the cluster default) and an optional wave plan (strategy sequential|rack-staged, stages ladder such as 1, 50%, 100%; blank inherits). Rack-staged is planned by the worker from the installed topology inventory (<install_root>/current/inventory/topology.tsv, node/SU/rack -- the same file the peers' scheduler labels come from): stage one puts one node in every rack at wave_size (the only stage that loads the seeds), later stages grow every rack to the next rung at fill_wave_size, racks round-robin across SUs; with no topology it falls back to sequential and says so in the log. When the fleet snapshot (<state>/p2p-snapshots/<cluster>.json) is under an hour old the plan also counts nodes that already hold the image toward each rack's rungs (a rack with a copy gets no seed wave), seeds each rack from the reachable peer with the most verified images, and puts unreachable nodes and roster holders in the rack's last stage. Every rollout watches each active download's written bytes: one that has not moved for stall_seconds (default 600, 0 = off) is stopped and relaunched, then deferred as stalled_<N>s_after_<L>_launches once it has used max_launches, instead of holding its wave to the timeout. Each node also enforces download_timeout_seconds (default 3600) on its own transfer -- dfget is killed when it passes -- and a launch replaces a running download older than that instead of re-adopting it; a wave that times out stops the downloads it gives up on. Launch is confirm-gated and enqueues an ordinary distribute operation through POST /api/p2p/operations tagged with the campaign name; the worker preheats the seeds then rolls out in waves. One operation runs at a time (409 otherwise). Re-launching is idempotent: nodes holding the pinned image are skipped by receipt.

entries.title: Rollouts
entries.summary: Pull distribution: put one catalog image onto racks through the node agents, rung by rung, and steer it while it runs.
entries.description: A rollout puts one pinned catalog image onto the racks you choose without opening an SSH session to any node. Rack Status writes each node's desired-state document into the directory the origin serves; the agent on the node fetches the image through its local Dragonfly peer, verifies it against the pin, installs it and reports back through the cluster's metrics. Each rack is released rung by rung -- by default one node first, which seeds the rack, then half, then all -- so most nodes pull from rack-mates rather than the app server. A rollout is a durable run: it survives a restart of Rack Status, and while it runs you can cancel it (nodes still downloading are told to stop; installed nodes keep the image), retry one node or every deferred node, and change the pacing, which applies from the next tick. A node with no live agent, one that keeps failing, or one that overruns its budget is deferred rather than holding its rack.
features: Rack-staged release with a live per-node view
Cancel, retry a node, retry every deferred node, change pacing -- all on a running rollout
Preview: each rack's members, live agents and current holders before starting
Survives a restart of Rack Status and resumes where it was
No SSH: desired-state documents out, agent metrics back

steps: Pin the image in Catalog.
Choose the image and the racks, and adjust the stage ladder, budget and racks in flight if needed.
Click Preview to see each rack's members, live agents and current holders, then Start rollout and confirm.
Open the rollout to follow each rack's rungs and nodes; Retry deferred nodes once the cause is fixed.

tips: Racks only take part if their nodes run the pull agent; a node without a live agent is deferred as no_agent.
Starting the same image on the same racks while that rollout is running opens the running one instead of a second.
Pull rollouts need Desired-state directory and Origin URL set in Dragonfly Settings.

aria.label: Rollouts
aria.description: Pull rollouts of a catalog image onto racks, with cancel, retry and pacing while they run.

entries.aiContext: Rollouts are NVIS-P2P pull rollouts (backend p2p_rollout.py, /api/p2p/rollouts; design docs/DESIGN_p2p-pull-agent.md). A rollout is a workflow-engine run of the built-in nvis-p2p-rollout workflow whose single native step is the coordinator; it is registered resumable, so a Rack Status restart resumes it. Start: POST /api/p2p/rollouts {image, racks, pacing:{stages, budget_seconds, max_active_racks}} (action p2p:rollout_start); the plan fixes the image pin from the cluster's catalog and each rack's members in tray order from the server's node inventory (cluster snapshot nodes[], placed by the rack-mapping mode and naming templates). The coordinator writes <desired_dir>/<node>.json (schema_version 1, generation, origin, images) and reads nvis_p2p_agent_up, nvis_p2p_agent_last_poll_timestamp_seconds, nvis_p2p_image_state and nvis_p2p_image_failures_total from the cluster's metrics_url (VictoriaMetrics); a node's report counts only once its agent has acted on the generation written for it. Rungs per rack from the stage ladder (1, 50%, 100% -> 1, 9, 18 of 18); max_active_racks racks at a time; nodes deferred as no_agent, failed_<n>x or timeout. Controls on a live run: POST .../cancel (p2p:rollout_cancel; withdraws the image from nodes still downloading), POST .../retry {nodes} (p2p:rollout_retry; empty = all deferred; rewrites the document with a new generation), PUT .../pacing (p2p:rollout_pace). A second start with the same image and racks joins the live run (idempotency key). GET /api/p2p/rollouts/plan previews members, live agents and holders.
